explain.say: Today we are learning powerful ways to find data in spreadsheets. We will look at VLOOKUP and XLOOKUP first. These functions help you search for information in tables.

VLOOKUP searches vertically, meaning it always looks down the first column. The search value must always be in the leftmost column of your data range. For example, if you search for an ID, the ID must be the first column.

XLOOKUP is the modern, more flexible replacement for VLOOKUP. It lets you search in any column and return data from any other column. This removes the strict requirement about the first column. For instance, you can search by Name and return the ID.

INDEX and MATCH work together for maximum flexibility. MATCH finds the position number of a value in a row or column. INDEX then retrieves the value at that specific position number. This combination avoids the left-to-right limitation of VLOOKUP.

In a real job scenario, you might be matching employee IDs to find their departmental budget. You use XLOOKUP to find the ID in one list and pull the corresponding budget from another list. This saves significant manual cross-referencing time.

explain.say: A common mistake is using VLOOKUP when the lookup column is not the first one. This will cause the function to return an error or incorrect data. Always ensure your search key is the leftmost item in your selected range.

items: Fix: Always check that the search column is first.

faq.q: Why is XLOOKUP considered an upgrade to VLOOKUP?
faq.a: XLOOKUP is more flexible because it does not require your search column to be the very first column in your data set. It also handles errors more intuitively than older functions. You might also ask: What is the difference between XLOOKUP and VLOOKUP? Or, How do I search data without it being in the first column?

faq.q: When should I use INDEX-MATCH instead of XLOOKUP?
faq.a: INDEX-MATCH is useful if you are working in a very old version of spreadsheet software that does not support XLOOKUP. It is also a fundamentally strong method that many professionals are trained on. You might also ask: Is INDEX-MATCH as good as XLOOKUP? Or, How do I combine INDEX and MATCH?

faq.q: What does the 'range' argument mean in these functions?
faq.a: The range specifies the entire block of cells where your data is located. You must select the correct columns and rows for the function to read the data from. You might also ask: How do I select a range? Or, What are the boundaries for the data?

faq.q: Can these functions handle text values or only numbers?
faq.a: These functions are designed to handle both text and numerical values correctly, as long as the data type is consistent across the column. If the data types mismatch, the function will likely return an error. You might also ask: Does it work for product codes? Or, Can I mix letters and numbers?

faq.q: What is the difference between looking up a single value versus multiple values?
faq.a: These functions are primarily designed to look up one specific value at a time. If you need to perform the lookup for many values, you usually need to drag the formula down or use array formulas. You might also ask: Can I do a bulk lookup? Or, How do I apply this to a whole column?

quiz.say: If you want to find the salary based on an employee's name, and the name column is not the first column, which function is best?
quiz.why: XLOOKUP allows you to specify the lookup column and the return column independently, ignoring the order.

wrong.0: While INDEX-MATCH works, XLOOKUP is the most direct and modern solution for this scenario.
wrong.1: FILTER is for returning multiple matching rows, not for a single, precise lookup.
wrong.3: VLOOKUP fails because it forces the search value to be in the absolute first column.

quiz.say: You need to find the score for 'Beta' from a table where 'Beta' is in the third column. Which combination should you use?
quiz.why: MATCH finds the position of 'Beta' within the NameRange, and INDEX retrieves the score at that exact position.

wrong.1: VLOOKUP would fail because 'Beta' is not in the first column of the data range.
wrong.2: This is a valid alternative, but the question specifically tests the INDEX-MATCH structure.
wrong.3: MATCH only returns a number (the position), not the actual score value.
